articles.title: Celebrity plastic surgeon reveals when it's too soon for a facelift, and when waiting can backfire
articles.summary: Dr. Terry Dubrow reveals why Kris Jenner's public facelift is driving 38-year-olds to seek facelift surgery they don't yet need.
articles.body: When it comes to getting a facelift, timing may be everything. Going under the knife too soon could mean having surgery before it’s necessary — but waiting too long can also backfire, according to celebrity plastic surgeon Dr. Terry Dubrow. During an episode of Josh Peck’s podcast, "Good Guys," the Beverly Hills-based surgeon said some women are jumping the gun and getting the procedure too soon. CHEAP SURGERY OVERSEAS MAY COME WITH DEVASTATING COMPLICATIONS, DOCTORS WARN "For those people in their 30s who want some skin tightening, they need to wait, 'cause there will be the technology that will allow early facelifts without cutting," he said. Dubrow also mentioned Kris Jenner’s recent facelift, which may have motivated women to seek out the procedure based on her results. "That made facelifts like, ‘Oh, Kris Jenner did it and made it public. Now it's cool. Everybody get a facelift,’" he said. "So then you're seeing 38-year-old people in your office wanting a facelift, and you go, ‘OK, hold on a second. You don't even need a facelift. You need to wait, because, you know, a facelift is incisions and scars, and elevating up the skin, numbness and all sorts of potential things that can go wrong." MEN FACE NEW PRESSURE TO STAY ‘HOT’ AS THEY AGE — AND IT’S NOT JUST ABOUT LIVING LONGER Dubrow warned that if people have too many facelifts, "when it starts to relax, it can relax in weird ways." "You've all seen it — people who look pretty good, but there's something about the way their skin lies on their face that looks unnatural, and it ruins the whole look," he warned. "If you have early laxity, don't go in for your ‘Kris Jenner facelift.’ Still wait, because that technology is just around the corner." Conversely, the surgeon has warned that waiting too long — while relying on other nonsurgical fixes — can also backfire. "A lot of women are staying on the ‘nonsurgical treadmill’ for too long," Dubrow told Fox News Digital. DO RED LIGHT THERAPY AND COLD PLUNGES REALLY WORK? A DOCTOR REVEALS THE TRUTH "They keep adding filler, lasers and tightening treatments, when the real problem is that the deeper tissues have dropped." While it is possible to get a great result with a later-in-life facelift, the doctor pointed out that as the skin becomes looser, the tissues descend further, which may require more extensive surgery. "My feeling is that once those treatments stop producing a natural result, continuing to postpone surgery can actually make you look less natural." That’s not to say that nonsurgical treatments don’t have their place, he noted. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES "Fillers, lasers and tightening treatments can buy you time when they are used intelligently — but fillers cannot lift sagging tissue, and too much filler can make someone look distorted." "The right time should be based on your face, not the doctor’s menu." Aggressive energy treatments can also create scarring under the skin and make surgery more difficult later, Dubrow cautioned — "so, ask whether a treatment is truly delaying a facelift or just delaying the decision." CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER There is no "magic age" in terms of best results with a facelift, according to Dubrow. "For some women, it is their late 40s. For others, it is their 50s or 60s," he said. "It comes down to genetics, skin quality and what is happening along the jawline and neck." Advice for facelift timing can vary depending on what type of expert you see, and every specialist tends to see the problem through the treatments they perform, the doctor noted. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "A dermatologist may explain what can still be accomplished without surgery, and a board-certified plastic surgeon can tell you when those options have reached their limit … and when it is time to actually reposition the anatomy," he said. Ultimately, he suggests getting opinions from both sides. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "The right time should be based on your face, not the doctor’s menu," Dubrow said. "Choose what makes sense for your anatomy, your goals and your tolerance for surgery." "The best facelift is the one nobody knows you had, but the best advice often comes from hearing more than one point of view."

articles.title: Can tech really get you off your phone and into real life?
articles.summary: NewTree Social founder Maddy O'Connor built a community events app to help people discover local gatherings, wellness events and run clubs nearby.
articles.body: How many times have you picked up your phone to check one thing and found yourself still scrolling 30 minutes later? I know I've done it. Our phones make it incredibly easy to stay connected. Yet something interesting seems to be happening at the same time. Many people are looking for more reasons to put those phones down and spend time with other people in the real world. Run clubs are growing. Local gatherings are drawing attention. Phone-free events are popping up. People seem hungry for experiences that feel a little less like another feed. That raises an interesting question: Could the same technology that keeps pulling us online also help get us back into real life? That idea is behind NewTree Social, an early-stage community events app from 29-year-old founder Maddy O'Connor. She wants people to use their phones to discover something happening nearby, make a plan and then go experience it. And the timing may be right. RESTAURANTS BAN DINERS' PHONES DURING MEALS AS NO-SCROLL TREND GROWS: PUT IT AWAY OR ELSE NEW! 🩺 Free CyberGuy LIVE class: Get Better Healthcare With AI Saturday, September 26 at 11 a.m. ET / 8 a.m. PT Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will show you five practical ways AI can help you organize your health history, remember important appointment details, understand complicated medical information, research prescriptions and prepare smarter questions for your doctor. No technical experience is needed. Save your free spot at CyberGuyLive.com. More people are looking beyond the screen There is some real data behind this shift. Eventbrite's 2026 Social Study surveyed people ages 18 to 35 in the U.S. and U.K. It found that 79% planned to attend more events in 2026. Among Gen Z respondents, 46% said they were limiting screen time and 74% said in-person experiences were more important than digital ones. Now, keep in mind that this research comes from Eventbrite, a company whose business revolves around live events. Still, those numbers line up with something we are seeing play out in the real world. Eventbrite says phone-free experiences listed on its platform grew 567% globally between 2024 and 2025. Attendance at those events rose 121%. The company based those numbers on events that used "phone-free" terminology in their title or description. For people who have spent years with a smartphone within arm's reach, intentionally putting it away feels significant. It also creates an unusual opening for technology. Instead of asking how an app can keep you scrolling longer, what if the goal becomes helping you find something worth closing the app for? One young founder saw an opportunity That is where O'Connor comes in. She told CyberGuy that the idea for NewTree grew partly from her own experience living in Washington, D.C., without an established group of friends. Her experience changed depending on where she lived and whether she could find places where meeting new people felt natural. At the same time, she was watching interest grow around run clubs, wellness events, social clubs and other in-person experiences. So she started building around that behavior. NewTree is designed to help people discover local activities and meet others through something they already want to do. I think that part is important. Walking into a room of strangers solely because you are supposed to meet people can feel awkward. Walking into a fitness class, community event or gathering you already find interesting gives you a reason to be there before you ever introduce yourself. For someone who recently moved or simply wants to expand a social circle, that could make taking the first step a little easier. NewTree wants your scrolling to lead somewhere Open NewTree and the basic experience should feel familiar. There is a feed. You browse events nearby. You can RSVP and get reminders about something you want to attend. But the idea behind that feed is a little different. O'Connor comes from a graphic design background and told CyberGuy that she deliberately wanted NewTree to feel more like a social platform than a traditional events directory. The app currently focuses on community, fitness and wellness events around Tampa, St. Pete and Clearwater. Apple describes it as an app for discovering local events, RSVPing and meeting new people. Hosts can add photos and videos to event listings. Users can browse what is happening around them and RSVP from their phones. O'Connor also wants reviews to play a bigger role in what people discover. She says reviews of a host's events can affect how those events perform in the feed instead of simply sitting on a profile. There is something almost funny about the concept. You open another social-style app because you want to spend less of your social life inside apps. But maybe that is exactly the point. EXPERTS REVEAL WHY 'NONNAMAXXING' TREND MAY IMPROVE MENTAL, PHYSICAL HEALTH How NewTree says it is different NewTree is entering a crowded space. Meetup, Eventbrite and Facebook already help people discover events nearby, and both Meetup and Eventbrite offer personalized recommendations. So what is NewTree trying to do differently? O'Connor says she wants the experience to feel more like a social platform built specifically around getting people together in person. She also says reviews can influence how a host's events perform in the feed, so better-reviewed experiences can potentially receive greater visibility. During NewTree's early pilot, O'Connor is personally reviewing and approving hosts before their events can appear publicly. None of those ideas completely reinvents event discovery. The bet is that putting them together in a more curated, community-focused experience will give people another useful way to find things to do and meet people nearby. Whether that gives people enough reason to add NewTree to the apps they already use is one of the biggest things the company still has to prove. The real test starts after you close the app Here is what I would be watching. Does NewTree help people make plans they actually follow through on? Getting someone to download an app is one thing. Getting them to put on shoes, leave home and show up somewhere is much harder. The idea works if you spend a few minutes browsing NewTree, find something interesting and eventually put the phone back in your pocket because you have somewhere to go. It becomes a lot less interesting if people simply scroll through another feed filled with things they might someday do. O'Connor is very open about just how early NewTree is. She told CyberGuy that NewTree is pre-traction and pre-revenue. Tampa Bay is the starting point because she wants to prove that people will use the platform in one market before trying to expand throughout Florida and eventually nationwide. So there is a long way to go. But the behavior NewTree is betting on already appears to be taking shape. Safety has to follow you into the real world Of course, using an app to find events where you may meet strangers brings some very real safety questions. O'Connor says she has taken a hands-on approach during NewTree's MVP stage. She told CyberGuy that she personally reviews and approves hosts before their events can appear on the platform. Users can report content or other users and block people. Hosts can also remove or report attendees. NewTree's current support page says business profiles are reviewed before they can post. However, there is an important limitation. A verified badge means NewTree says it has confirmed that the business is who it claims to be. It does not mean NewTree is endorsing or guaranteeing a specific event. NewTree's terms go further. They say events are generally operated independently by outside hosts and that NewTree does not ordinarily perform criminal background checks or identity verification on users, attendees, hosts or organizers. So I would still do some homework before showing up at an unfamiliar event. Look up the organizer independently. Check the venue. If you are uncomfortable going alone, bring someone you trust. Technology can help you find people. It cannot remove all of the risks that come with meeting people you do not know. What happens to your location? Privacy deserves a close look too. O'Connor told CyberGuy that NewTree collects basic account information, including your name, email, date of birth and location. She says the app can use a saved profile location or, with your permission, your device location. She also said the information is stored through NewTree's Supabase database, with database-level access controls designed to limit who can access different information. When someone RSVPs to a free event, O'Connor says the host receives the attendee's name, email and location information so they can manage and communicate with attendees. 1 IN 6 ADULTS PLAGUED BY LONELINESS AS RESEARCHERS REVEAL LASTING IMPACT OF COVID PANDEMIC There is also an age-rating wrinkle Another detail could cause some confusion. Apple currently gives NewTree a 13+ age rating. NewTree itself says you must be at least 18 years old to create an account or use the platform. O'Connor told CyberGuy that Apple's 13+ label reflects its content-based App Store rating rather than the minimum age NewTree allows on the platform. So, despite what you may see on the App Store listing, NewTree says the service itself is for adults 18 and older. NewTree still has plenty to prove Right now, Apple lists NewTree as an iPhone app. O'Connor told CyberGuy that Android support is planned but not available yet. The business model is still taking shape too. O'Connor says she is leaning toward keeping the app free for users while eventually offering optional premium tools for businesses and hosts. Exactly what those paid features would include has not been decided. So I would look at NewTree for what it is today: a very early app built around a much larger change in the way some people are thinking about technology. What this means to you Most of us could probably use a few more reasons to put the phone down and do something in the real world. Our phones have become where we communicate, work, watch videos and fill just about every empty moment. Sometimes the screen starts taking the place of the experiences it was supposed to help us find. Maybe the better approach is expecting more from the technology we already use. If an app helps you discover a local event, try something you would never have considered or meet someone you otherwise never would have crossed paths with, the phone becomes the starting point. Then it can get out of the way. I like that idea. Use the technology to find something worth doing. Then look up from the screen and go do it. Kurt's key takeaways What stands out to me here is how good technology has become at keeping us looking down. Notifications pull us back in. Feeds always have something else waiting. Before you know it, another chunk of your day has disappeared into a screen. Now we are seeing signs that many people want something different. They still want technology, but they also want more opportunities to be around people in the real world. NewTree has a lot to prove. But I like the problem O'Connor is trying to solve. Your phone already knows how to keep you home and entertained for hours. Maybe the next really useful social app will be the one that gives you a good reason to leave. Would you use an app designed to get you off your phone and out meeting people, or does downloading another social app defeat the whole purpose? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com. articles.title: ‘Once an alcoholic, always an alcoholic’ is outdated. Here’s why
articles.summary: Brad Pitt’s reported return to drinking in “a more restrained manner” has fueled debate around what constitutes recovery from alcohol use disorder.
articles.body:
EDITOR'S NOTE: If you or someone you know is struggling with substance abuse, call the US Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration's National Helpline at 800-662-HELP (4357) and find more resources here .

Brad Pitt's recent revelation that he's drinking again in "a more restrained manner," after seven years of sobriety following heavy drinking , sparked intense pushback. The actor's past behavior aside, the larger controversy was in challenging the long-held idea that someone who struggled with alcohol in the past can't ever drink normally — that recovery is defined solely by sobriety.

The controversy Pitt stepped into comes down to old versus relatively new approaches to dealing with drinking problems. What makes someone "recovered" from alcohol addiction has seen "an evolution in health care," said Dr. Smita Das, addiction psychiatrist in the Addiction Medicine Dual Diagnosis Clinic at Stanford University in California.

Relevant medical fields in recent years have widely embraced the idea of a spectrum of recovery, including sobriety and non-abstinence, but some clinicians, abstinence support organizations (most notably Alcoholics Anonymous), and patients with alcohol issues haven't caught up to the science — or are downright opposing it.

Pitt simply gave voice to the expanded understanding of recovery from what is commonly called alcohol addiction or alcoholism, but has been officially known as alcohol use disorder , or AUD, since 2013, according to the DSM-5. That's the fifth edition of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders — the authoritative handbook of mental disorders published by the American Psychiatric Association and used by mental health professionals in the United States.

The body of research on non-abstinent recovery has been growing as well. A small study in February examined how low to moderate drinking can be part of successful recovery for some. Compared with the abstinent group in that study, those who continued to drink felt more confident they could limit their intake. Participants who drank also felt that positive life changes and supportive relationships bolstered their efforts to maintain recovery.

In a larger 2025 study about non-abstinent recovery, about 1,900 participants reported drinking in the past month — and their health and functioning were similar to those of abstinent participants, though they were slightly more likely to be experiencing psychological distress.

Redefining alcohol use disorder and recovery

Alcohol use disorder is defined by the DSM-5 as "frequent or heavy alcohol drinking that becomes difficult to control and leads to problems such as in relationships, work, school, family, or other areas."

Someone can have mild, moderate or severe AUD depending on how many criteria they've experienced in the past year. This definition was a broader move away from previous DSMs' binary diagnoses of alcohol abuse and alcohol dependence. The "abuse" diagnosis required that a patient was experiencing severe or dangerous consequences such as alcohol-related legal problems or failure to fulfill major obligations. The "dependence" diagnosis referred to serious but less severe issues, such as abandoned interests and repeatedly failed attempts to quit drinking.

The DSM-5 definition of AUD supports the idea that sobriety "is a part of the definition of recovery, but it is not the whole thing," Das said — since patients can also reach remission by reducing drinking and whatever criteria that led to their diagnosis.

Researchers with the US National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism, or NIAAA, published a paper on a new definition of recovery from AUD in 2022 — calling it a process or outcome in which someone pursues or achieves both remission from AUD and cessation of heavy drinking.

Remission requires that a patient have no AUD criteria besides craving. Someone who hasn't had any criteria for up to three months is in initial remission — three months to one year is early remission, one to five years is sustained, and more than five years is stable. For men, cessation of heavy drinking means having no more than four standard drinks on a single day or 14 drinks weekly, and for women, maximum three drinks on one day or seven drinks weekly, the authors wrote.

The fulfillment of basic needs also factors into recovery, the authors added, as do enhancements or improvements in social support, spirituality, physical and mental health, and other aspects of well-being.

Before, while some studies had examined non-abstinent recovery in various ways, there wasn't an operational or measurable definition that would help researchers better chart and study recovery. This lack meant "we really had no systematic studies on what constitutes recovery, how long it lasts and, more importantly, how to improve recovery," said Dr. George Koob, NIAAA director and senior author of the paper. He and his coauthors worked with other researchers, clinicians and recovery specialists and incorporated the DSM-5 criteria.

The NIAAA definition has been accepted by many medical authorities and has been facilitating research, as the authors hoped, experts said.

The DSM-5 and NIAAA work increase access to care by not making patients feel like they have to be perfect to be considered recovered, which can be intimidating and prevent effort to heal, experts said. The work also lowers barriers in technical ways — the ability to be diagnosed with mild or moderate AUD makes you eligible for insured care before you hit rock bottom and need more expensive and intensive help. Not defining recovery by abstinence only is also aiding efforts to develop or broaden access to AUD medications .

Abstinence works best for most people, experts say. And those choosing abstinence experience the most progress in physical health, quality of life and psychosocial functioning, which is the ability to manage one's daily life, psychological well-being and social environment, the NIAAA researchers wrote. But, they added, a growing body of evidence shows that remission from heavy drinking also is linked to meaningful, long-term improvements.

Another study, from 2019 , found those who achieved abstinence and people who achieved just remission from heavy drinking had similar health care costs five years after treatment, and similar psychosocial functioning at one year and nine years post treatment. A 2025 study on recovery attempts as defined by NIAAA, however, found that participants who still drank were more likely to relapse.

There isn't much research on predictors for who can drink normally, said Das, who is also a clinical professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Stanford's School of Medicine. But per her clinical experience and the 2025 study, light or moderate consumption of alcohol may be more feasible for people who didn't have severe AUD, for those who don't have underlying mental health issues or have healed or learned to manage them, for those who have been sober for years, or for individuals no longer in the situation in which they started drinking.

Of course, regarding overall health, no amount of alcohol is good for you, as even low consumption has been linked with higher risk for issues including dementia , cancer , high blood pressure and stroke .

'Once an alcoholic, always an alcoholic'

Much of the general public, however, hasn't caught up to these developments, which remain strongly discouraged and criticized by the abstinence support group space — especially proponents of AA.

The ideas of "once an alcoholic, always an alcoholic" and that abstinence is the only way to recovery stem from the predominant messaging and influence of AA, which began in 1935, said Dr. Michael Joshua Ostacher, a member of the American Psychiatric Association's Council on Addiction Psychiatry.

"'Alcoholic' is a term that's adopted by Alcoholics Anonymous to identify its own members, and by which their own members identify themselves," added Ostacher, who is also a professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Stanford's School of Medicine.

This approach is based on the idea that AUD is an incurable illness, Das said, and, in some people's minds, that all cases result from a brain already prone to addiction. Hence the belief — and often lived experience — that even just a sip of alcohol can make anyone relapse regardless of any recovery work done or number of years sober. These factors have created a culture in which people who return to normal drinking are often told by sober people that if they can do so without their consumption becoming excessive and destructive, they were never an "alcoholic" or "true addict" in the first place — maybe just someone who was emotionally dependent on alcohol.

On one hand, while the "always an alcoholic" phrase "is clinically outdated," for vulnerable people it's a protective behavioral boundary preventing them from attempting risky experiments, Das said.

Abstinence and 12-step programs, including AA, have proven to be significantly effective for many people worldwide, Ostacher said — AA had nearly 2 million active members and more than 120,000 groups worldwide as of 2021, according to the organization's data .

On the other hand, the debate reflects a clash between the medical and cultural frameworks used to make sense of addiction, Das said.

"Addiction is not universally a fixed, unchangeable neurological state," Das said. Someone can meet criteria for severe AUD at age 21, and then, with treatments, brain maturation, lifestyle changes and/or years of abstinence, be diagnosis-free at age 40. The brain is a muscle with adaptable neurocircuitry that can be healed by those interventions, Das added — but there are also people whose deeply affected neural reward and habit pathways may not heal entirely.

"To claim someone who went through that hard work 'never had a problem' minimizes the real medical struggle they overcame," Das said. "It would be like telling someone who was obese and now thin after a lot of hard work, that they never were obese."

Additionally, AA and its principles don't work for everyone, experts said. But "from AA's perspective, it didn't work for them because they didn't work the program hard enough, or they weren't honest enough to work the program," Ostacher said.

A setting wherein one drink is a violation of recovery and necessitates starting over can make people feel ashamed, even if they're really trying — which can lead to more serious relapses. Kenneth Anderson, a 68-year-old man from Philadelphia, said, "I never drank as much in my life as when I was in AA."

The requirement for belief in a higher power also doesn't resonate with everyone. Anderson, an atheist, added that he felt the insistence that "humans are powerless and can only be rescued from alcohol by an omnipotent deity" was a "terrible, damaging message." Anderson struggled with AUD from roughly the 1980s to 2000s, but now has limited his drinking to heavy consumption on one day at home every one or two months if he wants, while practicing other important elements of recovery. For him, those include managing the online HAMS (Harm Reduction, Abstinence and Moderation Support) group he founded that has more than 13,000 members.

Importantly, various factors contribute to AUD and may not be addressed by AA, experts said. Those include genetics, neurological vulnerabilities, life stressors and mental health issues — 50% of people with a substance use disorder have a mental health condition.

When a patient who has recovered and improved their life asks Das about drinking again, she asks about their true motives, any potential risks and the behaviors that sustain their goals.

Sometimes a patient wants to have a drink with friends to feel included or less anxious. In those cases, Das might recommend they buy a mocktail or practice coping skills instead. If they're thinking alcohol could help them unwind, Das encourages them to consider what else might relax them and maybe even benefit them in other ways.

Part of the risk is that alcohol inherently reduces our ability to make wise judgments, including whether we have had enough or more than planned, Das said. And even if you can drink and still be clinically recovered, there may be other reasons to choose abstinence — maybe your issues harmed loved ones, and they would be emotionally destabilized or offended by you drinking again.

"If they are very set on returning to drinking, then we have a conversation about, 'OK, what are the things that you're going to do to try to reduce the consequences that occurred before?'" Das said. She reviews with the patient the DSM-5 criteria they previously met so that they can recall the situations that led to problems — for example, if drinking alone makes them drink too much and spiral emotionally. "So then we say, 'OK, drinking is only in social situations, and you have a limit,'" Das added. She and the patient then schedule follow-up appointments and keep a log of how everything's going.

If you drink, watch for signs that it may be becoming problematic again, experts said — such as if you're often not sticking to your rules or making them too flexible. If you're currently struggling with alcohol, know that 1 in 10 Americans ages 12 and older have AUD, Das said. Discussing it honestly can lead you to the right treatments : outpatient or inpatient rehab, medications and therapies including cognitive behavioral therapy with relapse prevention, which is the most used therapy.

Both abstinence and moderation support groups can be helpful. Moderation Management , a member-run nonprofit founded in 1994, is a popular and professionally endorsed alternative to the abstinence approach. It has virtual and in-person sessions and encourages members to follow a nine-step program. They include doing an initial 30-day period of sobriety, examining how drinking has affected one's life, making positive lifestyle changes and setting moderate drinking limits.

articles.title: Kim Kardashian’s new health scare: What is esophagitis?
articles.summary: Kim Kardashian revealed in the trailer for Season 8 of “The Kardashians” that she’s facing a new health condition.
articles.body: Kim Kardashian revealed in the trailer for Season 8 of “The Kardashians” that she’s facing a new health condition. “I have something called esophagitis,” Kardashian says in one clip from the trailer, released Thursday. In another clip, Kris Jenner, Kardashian’s mother, says the diagnosis “makes me want to cry.” According to the Mayo Clinic, esophagitis is inflammation of the tissue lining the esophagus, the muscular tube that carries food and drink from the mouth to the stomach. Later in the trailer, Kardashian is shown lying in a hospital bed, hooked up to machines, while someone off camera asks whether that is what her father, Robert Kardashian, died of. Robert Kardashian died of esophageal cancer in 2003, at age 59. Dr. Stuart Spechler, a gastroenterologist at Baylor University Medical Center and a member of the American Gastroenterological Association, said that there are many types of esophagitis and that Kardashian did not specify which type she has. “Far and away the most common form is reflux esophagitis, which is a complication of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD),” he said. In those patients, Spechler explained, the mechanisms that normally keep stomach acid from moving back up the esophagus are defective, allowing refluxed acid to irritate and damage the esophagus. Common symptoms include heartburn and regurgitation. Some patients with reflux esophagitis go on to develop Barrett’s esophagus, a condition in which chronic acid exposure damages the esophagus’s normal lining and causes it to be replaced by cells resembling those found in the intestine and stomach, Spechler said. “It is a risk factor for developing a type of esophageal cancer called esophageal adenocarcinoma,” he said of Barrett’s esophagus. Still, Spechler noted that esophagitis is only a small risk factor for esophageal cancer and that women are less likely than men to develop both Barrett’s esophagus and esophageal cancer. “Most patients who have GERD and reflux esophagitis do not have Barrett’s esophagus, and most patients with Barrett’s esophagus do not develop cancer,” Spechler said. Both conditions are diagnosed using endoscopy, a procedure that lets doctors examine the esophagus and take biopsies to check for abnormalities. Patients with Barrett’s esophagus typically undergo regular endoscopies, Spechler said, “to identify early changes that indicate higher risk for developing cancer.” In 2019, the Kardashian family helped open the Robert G. Kardashian Center for Esophageal Health at UCLA, established as “a center for holistic, patient-centered treatment, research and education related to disorders of the esophagus,” according to a news release. The family said at the time that it planned to launch fundraising efforts to support the center’s key initiatives. “Our family is proud to pay tribute to our father by partnering with UCLA Health to establish the Robert G. Kardashian Center for Esophageal Health,” Kardashian said, according to the 2019 release. “We look forward to working with our longtime family friend, Dr. Eric Esrailian, the Melvin and Bren Simon Digestive Diseases Center, and the UCLA Vatche and Tamar Manoukian Division of Digestive Diseases to build the best program of its kind in the country.” She added: “We hope to save lives and help the community for many years to come in honor of our father.”

Esophageal cancer occurs when malignant cells form in the tissues lining the esophagus, according to the National Cancer Institute. articles.title: The first mRNA flu shot is now available. Here’s who can get it.
articles.summary: People looking to get their annual flu shot this fall may find a new option alongside the usual vaccines: an mRNA flu shot. Not everyone is eligible, however.
articles.body: The first mRNA flu shot is now available, but not everyone is eligible. Moderna’s mFlusiva is the first flu vaccine in the United States to use messenger RNA technology, the same platform used in Pfizer and Moderna’s Covid shots. Scientists have long been interested in using mRNA against the flu because the vaccines can be made faster, potentially making it easier to keep up with changing flu strains. It’s too early to predict how severe the upcoming flu season will be and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention hasn’t started tracking cases yet. The CDC recommends getting vaccinated by the end of October. In a late-stage clinical trial, published in the New England Journal of Medicine in May, mFlusiva was found to be about 27% more effective than a standard flu shot. The Food and Drug Administration approved mFlusiva in August for people 50 and older, clearing the way for the shot to reach pharmacies in time for this year’s flu season. Pharmacies, however, say the new vaccine is already causing confusion among some patients about who can get it, how it compares with traditional flu shots and where people will be able to find it. Here’s what you need to know: Who can get the new mRNA flu shot? The mRNA vaccine is available only for people 50 and older. “If you have not celebrated your 50th birthday, this vaccine should be of no interest to you,” said Emlah Tubuo, an independent pharmacist in Ohio. The FDA granted traditional approval for adults 50 to 64 and accelerated approval for people 65 and older, with Moderna required to conduct another trial in that age group. People who do not want the mRNA vaccine can still get a traditional flu shot. The additional trial in adults 65 and older stems from a controversy that nearly derailed the vaccine’s approval. In a large clinical trial, Moderna compared mFlusiva with a standard-dose flu shot in people 65 and older, even though the CDC recommends a high-dose flu shot for that age group. The FDA initially refused to review Moderna’s application over that issue before reversing course and agreeing to a post-approval clinical trial. In June, the FDA’s independent vaccine advisory panel unanimously recommended the approval of the vaccine for older adults. People younger than 50 won’t be able to get mFlusiva this flu season. Instead, they can get one of the other flu vaccines approved for their age group. How is the mRNA shot different from a traditional flu shot? The biggest difference is how the vaccines teach the immune system to recognize influenza. Most traditional flu shots use a deactivated version of the virus — often grown in eggs — to teach the immune system how to fight it. MFlusiva uses a small snippet of genetic code to train the body to recognize and fight the flu virus. The mRNA from the vaccine is then broken down and does not remain in the body. “It’s like a temporary instruction to your immune system to alert your body’s natural defense to recognize influenza,” Tubuo said. It takes about two weeks after vaccination to build protection. One point of confusion among patients, according to Brigid Groves, a pharmacist with the American Pharmacists Association, is whether mFlusiva also protects against Covid. It doesn’t. The vaccine only targets the flu and is separate from Moderna’s combination Covid and flu vaccine, which was approved by the European Union in April. Like the traditional seasonal flu vaccines this year, Moderna’s shot is a trivalent vaccine, targeting two influenza A strains and one influenza B strain. Another difference is that Moderna’s vaccine can be made faster, said Dr. William Schaffner, an infectious disease specialist at Vanderbilt University Medical Center. Scientists typically have to choose which flu strains to target months before flu season begins, leaving time to manufacture millions of doses. Traditional flu vaccines can take about six months to produce, while Moderna says mFlusiva can be made in two to three months. That shorter timeline, Schaffner said, allows them to wait longer before choosing which strains to target, giving them a better idea of which ones are likely to circulate. Is the mRNA shot safe and effective? Published data from a Phase 3 clinical trial suggests mFlusiva should work better than a standard-dose flu shot.More than 40,000 adults 50 and older across 11 countries, including the United States, participated in the trial. The trial found mFlusiva was about 27% more effective than the standard-dose vaccine at preventing laboratory-confirmed illness. FDA reviewers did not identify any serious safety problems with the vaccine. Rates of side effects — such as injection-site pain, fatigue and headaches — were more common in the mFlusiva group but still mild to moderate. Schaffner said the higher rate of side effects may be “a reflection of the vigor with which the immune system responds to the vaccine.” Will insurance cover mFlusiva? MFlusiva is reaching pharmacies without a formal recommendation from the CDC or its vaccine advisory committee, a step typically needed to require insurers to cover vaccines for free. A spokesperson for AHIP, a trade group for health insurers, said it expects most private insurers will cover the vaccine. Dorit Reiss, a vaccine policy expert at University of California Law San Francisco, said Medicare is required to fully cover the cost of FDA-approved seasonal flu shots. Reiss said it remains unclear, however, how widely Medicaid will cover the new shot this season, as the program typically requires a formal recommendation from the CDC’s vaccine advisory committee. According to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, mFlusiva has a price tag of around $171 per dose without insurance. Depending on the pharmacy, the cost could be as low as $154, according to GoodRx. Where can people get it? As with any vaccines, whether you can get the shot right away will depend on your local pharmacy’s current stock and delivery schedule. In a statement, a Moderna spokesperson said the company has begun shipping doses of mFlusiva across the U.S. Amy Thibault, a CVS Health spokesperson, said mFlusiva is available at its U.S. pharmacies. A Walgreens spokesperson said it expects to begin receiving shipments of the vaccine any day now, although it’ll be available to patients in “limited quantities” this season. Tubuo, the Ohio pharmacist, said that demand for mFlusiva is currently low, noting that it is still early in the season and most people do not seek vaccination until October.
